summary.text: An outcome is a possible result of an experiment or trial, and all of the possible outcomes together form the sample space.
Different outcomes are mutually exclusive, so only one occurs on each trial, and outcomes should not be confused with events, which are groups of outcomes.
Outcomes can have probabilities between zero and one, but in a continuous distribution each individual outcome has zero probability.

facts.value: Four outcomes: (H, T), (T, H), (T, T) and (H, H)

facts.value: An event containing exactly one outcome

items.prompt: You flip a coin twice and win if at least one flip is heads. Which of the four possible outcomes is not a winning one?

options.label: (H, T)
(T, H)
(H, H)
(T, T)

items.explain: The event 'at least one heads' contains every outcome except (T, T).

items.prompt: For one die roll, which of these is a single outcome rather than a group of outcomes?

options.label: The roll is an even number
The roll shows exactly a four
The roll is bigger than two
The roll is one of the odd numbers

items.explain: An event is a group of outcomes; a single result is one outcome, and an event holding exactly one outcome is an elementary event.

items.prompt: A dart lands at a random real-number position along a ruler. What is the chance it lands at exactly 3.5?

options.label: Zero, because single outcomes have no probability here
A small positive amount, shared by all positions
One half, because it either lands there or not
It cannot be said, because the ruler is too long

items.explain: In a continuous distribution individual outcomes all have zero probability; only ranges of outcomes can have non-zero probabilities.

items.prompt: Which of these experiments is hard to describe with equally likely outcomes?

options.label: Tossing a thumb tack to see if its point lands up or down
Shuffling and drawing one card from a deck
Rolling an ordinary six-sided die
Tossing an ordinary coin once

items.explain: Coins, dice and shuffled cards are usually assumed equally likely, but a thumb tack has no symmetry to suggest its two outcomes are.

items.prompt: Two coin flips both come up heads. How many different events can that single outcome be part of?

options.label: Just one, named after the outcome itself
None, unless it is the only outcome
Only events that hold exactly two outcomes
Many different events at once

items.explain: A single outcome can be a part of many different events.

items.prompt: At a casino a player secretly shaves a die so some faces come up more often. What is this player doing to the outcomes?

options.label: Forcing them to rule each other out
Introducing a systematic departure from equal likelihood
Turning them into events
Raising each one's chance past certainty

items.explain: Games of chance implicitly assume equally likely outcomes, and cheaters try to introduce systematic deviations from that, such as with shaved dice.
